title: Journaling and prayer walks
hookLine: evangelicals who keep prayer journals and walk their streets praying for each house

cards: A spiral notebook with a cracked cover, half full. Some pages are lists: a name, a diagnosis, a job interview, a daughter's exam. Next to a few of them, in different ink, written later, a date and one word: answered.
Next to others, nothing yet. It's a prayer journal, and evangelical Christians are among those who keep them.
Some of them also take the notebook in a pocket and walk their own street slowly, praying for each house they pass. Two habits, one on paper and one on foot.

teach.h: WRITE THE VISION, MAKE IT PLAIN.
teach.b: Start with the paper. When the prophet Habakkuk waits for God's answer, the answer begins: "Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it." Write it down, plainly, so it can be carried.
The Psalms themselves are written prayers, complaint and praise on the same page.
In one of them, the writer is so troubled he can't sleep, and then he turns: "I will remember the works of the LORD: surely I will remember thy wonders of old." That's what a prayer journal is for.
Memory is slippery, and a page isn't. Months later you can read what you were afraid of, see what happened, and see how your own prayers changed. Now the feet.
Genesis gives Enoch one short line: "And Enoch walked with God." A life with God, pictured as a walk. Prayer walkers take the picture outdoors.
They go slowly, eyes open, and let what they see become the prayer. A swing set: the children on this street. A for-sale sign: whoever's leaving, and whoever's coming.
A wheelchair ramp. A window that stays dark. Matthew says that when Jesus went through the towns and saw the crowds, "he was moved with compassion on them."
He saw first. Walking slowly is a way of seeing. Some people bring the two habits together.
They walk, come home and write down the houses they prayed for, and later, sometimes, what happened.

how: Some evangelical Christians keep a notebook of prayer requests and note later when and how they were answered; churches and small groups also organize prayer walks, walking a neighborhood slowly and praying for the homes, schools and businesses they pass.

games.q: what does “journaling and prayer walks” mean?
o: walking pilgrimages to holy sites, with a travel log
a diary of daily moods kept alongside hikes
prayers written down, and prayers walked house by house

"write the vision, and make it plain upon tables."
a prayer walk is done with eyes closed
it's done eyes open: what you see becomes the prayer.

games.q: you're the prophet Habakkuk. you've brought your complaint to God and climbed to your watchpost to wait. the answer comes. what are you told to do with it?
o: write the vision, and make it plain.
games.why: "write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it." written plainly, so it can be carried.

practice: If you're able, stand and walk, outside or slowly around the room; if you're sitting, walk your street in your mind, one house at a time. Notice one detail at each, a car, a toy, a porch light, and let it become the prayer.
If you pray, ask God's good for whoever lives there; if you don't, simply wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Journaling and prayer walks. Prayers written down to be remembered, and prayers walked, house by house, with eyes open.

orig.note: Hebrew: to walk, to go. Genesis 5:24 uses a form of it: Enoch walked with God.

carryVoice: Your line: pray as you walk. Eyes open, house by house. Rest well.
